uncited: This family covers hardware systems and computational methods that render volumetric data directly into physical space, creating images that occupy a 3D volume visible from multiple viewpoints without headgear.
It differs from standard rasterization or ray marching by projecting light into a physical medium (air, glass, or light fields) rather than onto a 2D sensor or screen.

It is distinct from [Voxel engines and games](47-voxel-engines-and-games.md) which simulate volume appearance on 2D displays, and from [Scientific and medical visualization](49-scientific-and-medical-visualization.md) which typically uses 2D slice views or volume rendering on monitors.
All methods in this family share the goal of mapping 3D voxel data $I(x,y,z)$ to a physical 3D light field.

The core challenge is resolving the "viewing space" vs. "drawing space" conflict: the medium used to generate voxels (e.g., gas, laser focus, holographic plane) often differs from the space where the user observes them.

**Spatial Mapping:** Transforming 3D voxel coordinates $(x,y,z)$ into 2D control signals (pixel buffers, SLM patterns, or scanner coordinates) synchronized with mechanical motion (rotation, scanning) or optical projection.
**Light Propagation Modeling:** Calculating how light interacts with voxels, including attenuation, reflection, and diffraction, to determine the intensity and phase required at the output plane.

**Temporal/Spatial Multiplexing:** Using persistence of vision (rotating mirrors, scanning beams) or optical superposition (holography) to create the illusion of a continuous 3D volume from discrete 2D slices or points.
Holographic display methods for volume data have evolved from early computer-generated holography (CGH) techniques.
Modern volumetric holography aims to visualize 3D datasets (medical, scientific) directly in 3D space.
